Envelopes In Ellipse

CurvesGeometryCoordinates
Game: A ray of light bounces around an elliptical mirror; watch what the bouncing lines touch.
How to play: Drag the four corners to change the mirror and drag T1 or T2 around its edge. Press Add reflection to follow the ray, then use Add 10, Add 100, Remove last, Remove all and Reset.
Look for the math

Bogomolny's applet lets a light ray bounce inside an ellipse again and again. The page says there are only three things the bouncing pieces can do. This page keeps the applet's draggable points and its buttons so you can see which one happens; there is no winning move.

One ray, many bounces

At each bounce the ray leaves the mirror at the same angle at which it arrived, measured against the tangent. The applet finds the next point in three steps: reflect the previous point in that tangent, turn the image through the bounce point to get the outgoing direction, and cut the ellipse again. The logic test compares this with the ordinary mirror formula on hundreds of mirrors and starting pairs; all 25-bounce paths agree to better than a thousandth of a board unit. Every generated point lies on the ellipse and every pair of incoming and outgoing pieces makes equal angles with the tangent.

The number that never changes

Let F1 and F2 be the two foci, separated by 2c. Reflect F1 in a piece of the ray to get F1', and call R = |F1' F2|. The same R comes out for every piece of one path: reflecting F2 in the next piece gives the same distance back to F1, which is the equality at the heart of the page's proof. The test checked this along all 360 starting directions, with eight bounces each.

R constant; a' = R/2; b'² = |a'² − c²|

When R > 2c, the confocal curve with foci F1, F2 and semi-axis a' is an ellipse. When R < 2c it is a hyperbola. In both cases the test checked the tangent equation n² = a'² l² ± b'² m² for every piece, where l x + m y + n = 0 is the piece's line in coordinates centred at the mirror. All three cases really occur, so the page's classification holds.

Three cases, one rule

If the first piece passes through a focus, the reflected ray goes through the other focus and then alternates between them: the test followed six such rays for twelve bounces each. Otherwise all pieces either cross the short segment between the foci or none of them does. The first choice gives an envelope of ellipses, the second an envelope of hyperbolas; the 360-direction scan found no path that switches between the two. The small drift in the focus case is expected: the page itself says that case is only partly checked because the points are hard to place exactly.

Small differences from the old applet

The applet chose T2 at a random angle, so this page fixes it to make a saved position replayable; you can drag it anywhere. Its Show boxes were off unless the page set a parameter. Dragging a point to the left half of the mirror triggers the old angle routine's habit of snapping it to the far-left point; that quirk is kept. Corners cannot be dragged within twelve units of the centre, and a ray that lands exactly on a diameter stops growing because the applet's circle-cutting routine rejects it. Neither changes the geometry of the pieces that are drawn.

Press Add 100, then tick Extended lines and Reflections for a proof: the dashed lines from the foci meet at two reflected points that are the same distance from the opposite focus, R.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
